edge.title: Meter politics at the junction
edge.setup: Late evening, it's about to rain. The auto outside refuses the meter and quotes a flat fare, double. There's no other auto in sight, and he knows all three of those facts.
move: Change where you stand. Walk 100m to the main road; scarcity was the only leverage he had.
Open an app and let him watch. The visible alternative resets the price more reliably than argument.
If you need the formal route: the refusal, auto number and location go to the Bengaluru Traffic Police app or 080-22868550. Mentioning you're noting the number often ends the matter.
Never start with anger. Start with the alternative — anger is a worse tool than a visible option.
edge.tell: If you're arguing about the price, you've already accepted that he's the only option.
edge.why: Price is set by alternatives, not by fairness. Every effective move here manufactures an alternative — distance, an app, a complaint channel — rather than appealing to rules. This is the whole of negotiation in miniature.
edge.variants: Same shape: surge pricing you can wait out, 'last room available' at a hotel desk, the mechanic who found three more problems.
edge.anchor: TOI Bengaluru reports a new automated system at Bengaluru airport to detect taxi lane violations, on a day it also ran a piece on the ₹1,500 airport cab fare and the Blue Line's new deadline.

lens.name: Second-order effects
lens.one_line: The first consequence of a change is usually obvious and usually not the one that matters.
lens.detail: First order: a metro line opens, your commute drops 40 minutes. Second order: everyone else's does too, so rents near the stations rise, which prices out the people the line was meant to serve, which changes who rides it. Most policy arguments are conducted entirely in first-order terms, which is why they keep surprising everyone.
elsewhere: A subsidy lowers a price, so demand rises, so the queue becomes the real cost.
A company bans a tool, so work routes through an unmonitored one.
Rent control holds rents, so landlords stop maintaining and supply shrinks.
lens.test: Ask 'and then what?' three times. The answer that surprises you is where the real story is.
lens.today: The RBI raised the repo rate to 5.5% and the Governor says cuts are off the table for now. The first-order effect is a higher EMI. Ask 'and then what?': lenders pass it on to floating-rate borrowers, home buyers defer purchases, and rents hold firm as more people keep renting. Fixed deposits start to pay more, so saving becomes the safer move for anyone not already carrying a loan.

moved.what: The RBI hiked the repo rate to 5.5% today and the Governor said rate cuts are off the table in the near term.
moved.so_what: If you have a floating-rate home or car loan, expect your EMI or tenure to go up at the next reset. Ask your lender which one changes, and don't plan a refinance around a cut that isn't coming. Fixed deposit rates are likely to rise, so hold off locking a long FD for a few weeks.

moved.what: Two transformer blasts in Bengaluru injured five people today, including a footpath transformer outside an Amazon office that injured two.
moved.so_what: With rain likely tonight, don't wait, park or shelter next to footpath transformer boxes. If one is sparking, leaking or open, walk away and report it to the power utility, don't wait to see whether it settles.

moved.what: A 'Chappal protest' against the SIR voter-roll revision, called for women's safety too, is set for Thursday 8 October in Bengaluru, with actor Prakash Raj joining.
moved.so_what: The reports don't name a venue, so check the Traffic Police advisory before you leave tomorrow. If you drive through the city centre, leave early or take the metro.

moved.what: Bengaluru airport is bringing in an automated system to detect taxi lane violations, and the Blue Line to the airport has a new deadline.
moved.so_what: Until the metro opens, the ₹1,500 airport cab stays the default. Book the ride before you land and use the designated taxi lane, since pickups outside it are now easier to catch.
